        never performed twice. Where a provider accepts an idempotency header,
        the relay sends one, after a capture shows it (rule 13).
    - **Turns survive a dropped model connection, compaction included.** This
      is harness-wide: every editor, the ACP agent, headless runs and nodes.
      It extends M106 lane R's retry table (429, 5xx, 504) and M101 lanes C1
      and C2's compaction path rather than adding a second retry layer, and
      their owners review it.
      - **A network failure pauses a turn; it never fails it.** A refused,
        reset or timed-out connection, a DNS or TLS failure, or a stream cut
        short is classified as a network failure. The turn shows "Paused:
        connection to api.meta.ai lost at 21:04, retrying (2 of 6)", with
        **Resume now** and **Stop**.
      - **Bounded retries, then waiting.** Up to `MODEL_RESUME_ATTEMPTS`
        retries with jittered backoff, sooner when the OS reports the network
        back or a free probe answers (Meta's `GET /v1/status`, D86.6). After
        them the turn stays paused, resumable, never failed, until the network
        returns or the user acts. A headless run keeps D65's deadline and then
        exits as incomplete (8) with its session to resume, never as failed.
      - **Resume from the last consistent point.** That is the last complete,
        validated item of the stream: a finished message part or a complete
        tool call. Text after it is discarded, never shown as final, and a
        tool call whose arguments arrived only in part is never run (D86).
        Tool calls that already ran are never run again: their results stay
        in the history the next request carries. Where a provider can resume
        a stream from a cursor (a capability in M95's record, set only after a
        capture), the harness resumes; otherwise it sends the request again
        from that point.
      - **The same accounting, nothing counted twice.** The cut attempt is
        settled once, from whatever usage it reported; with none, it stays an
        uncertain liability reserved at its worst case (M82). The retry is its
        own attempt with its own reservation inside D78's daily budget and
        M82's conversation cap, and the journal links the two (M102). The
        vendor may still bill a cut attempt; the reservation covers that, and
        the usage page shows both attempts. A D48 paid feature retried after a
        connection failure asks again, unless the failure is proved to have
        happened before the request was sent (DNS, connect or TLS).
      - **Compaction is atomic.** A compaction whose request fails is retried
        as compaction; the conversation is not changed until a validated
        summary replaces the compacted range in one step, so a cut never loses
        or half-applies history. If compaction keeps failing and the next
        request would overflow the context, the turn pauses instead of sending
        it.
      - **On Muse Code** the CLI owns its model connection. The harness
        recognises a turn that ended in a network-class error (from the MSP
        error frame, captured under rule 13), waits for the network and
        continues the same session, at most `MODEL_RESUME_ATTEMPTS` times, and
        asks Meta upstream for retries inside the CLI. **External agents** over
        ACP get the same continuation in their own session; each is billed as
        that agent bills.
    - **Fault injection proves it** (M110r lane Y4): an address change, a
      link flap, a partition in one or both directions, a long outage, relay
      loss and clock skew, each across a running job and a streaming turn,
      and a model stream cut mid-response and mid-compaction. Each run proves
      no lost work, no duplicate side effects and the correct state in every
      UI.

26. **Google Chrome is the host's browser** (the owner, 2026-10-05: "our os
    need chrome as the default browser for the host version"). This covers
    Muse Node OS (decision 24) and the native host install (decision 4).
    Research §4.11 has the sources.
    - **Not in our image.** Google's Terms of Service (effective 30 July 2026)
      forbid users to "copy, modify, distribute, sell, or lease any part of
      our services or software", and its licence is "personal". So no image,
      container or installer of ours carries Chrome.
    - **Installed at first boot, by the user's own click.** The first-boot
      setup (decision 24) and the host dashboard offer **Install Google
      Chrome**, with links to Google's Terms of Service and Chrome's
      Additional Terms. Accepting them is the user's click; no flag, seed
      file, cloud-init key or script accepts for them.
      - The node then adds Google's APT repository. It checks the signing key
        `https://dl.google.com/linux/linux_signing_key.pub` against the
        fingerprint Google publishes (`EB4C 1BFD 4F04 2F6D DDCC EC91 7721 F63B
D38B 4796`, "Google, Inc. (Linux Package Signing Authority)"), and
        refuses on any difference.
      - It installs `google-chrome-stable` and makes it the system's default
        browser, the handler for every link the host opens.
    - **ARM64 too.** Google now ships stable Chrome for Linux arm64 through
      the same Debian and RPM repositories, tested on a Raspberry Pi 5 (it
      reached the stable channel in July and August 2026). Chrome for Testing
      has published linux-arm64 builds since 153.0.8001.0, and its stable
      channel (154.0.8037.92 on 6 October 2026) lists them.
      - **Chromium as the fallback.** It is used only where Google's package
        does not install, for example a 32-bit system, which Muse Node OS
        never is, or when the user declines Google's terms. It comes from
        Debian's own `chromium` package and is still set as the default.
      - **The UI says so:** "Chromium (Google Chrome is not available here)",
        or "(you declined Google's terms)".
    - **Updated through Google's repository.** Chrome's updates are security
      updates: they install automatically like Debian's, by decision 24's
      update rules (staged at once, the browser restarted when idle). On Muse
      Node OS's read-only system, Chrome lives in decision 24's add-on layer,
      not in the signed image.
    - **Agents never drive the user's Chrome.** Automation (M81's browser
      check, over CDP) runs Google's Chrome for Testing: Google's own Chrome,
      built for automation, pinned per release, verified against its recorded
      digest and downloaded after consent (M81), on amd64 and now arm64. It
      gets a fresh private profile for every check and runs behind its own
      proxy. An auto-updating installed Chrome would change under M81's pin,
      and its profile holds the user's sign-ins, so the system Chrome is never
      automated: M81's rule stands.
    - **Two profiles, two policy sets, kept apart by the file system.**
      - **Automation:** the browser check runs inside the workspace's sandbox
        (decision 5) as the tools' user, with its own `/etc`. There, a managed
        policy file (`/etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed/`, Chrome's documented
        Linux location) turns off what automation never needs: sign-in, sync,
        the password manager, autofill, extensions, downloads and background
        mode.
        - It never sets a `Proxy…` policy or a cloud enrolment token, under
          which M81's check refuses to start.
        - Lane 0 captures which policy folder Chrome for Testing reads, and
          that its CDP pipe works under this policy.
      - **The user's Chrome** reads the host's own `/etc`. There the node
        writes only recommended policies, which the user can change: the
        start page is the node's web UI, and Chrome is the default browser.
        It writes no mandatory policy, so the browser stays the user's.
    - **A local screen, if the machine has one.** The host edition can start
      a kiosk session: a minimal Wayland compositor, `cage` (in Debian),
      running Chrome full-screen on the node's web UI at `https://localhost`.
      There, the node's certificate is trusted and passkeys work. A sign-in
      that opens a browser (Muse Code's browser sign-in, decision 7, or an
      OAuth flow) opens in that Chrome, which removes the headless sign-in
      problem on such machines.
    - **The container and rented-server editions** do not install Chrome:
      people reach them from their own browsers, and automation uses Chrome
      for Testing in the sandbox.

27. **Ready for agents out of the box, and set up for how the user works**
    (M110a0, M110os and M110t). The owner, 2026-10-05: "we need a first run
    questionaire to ask how the user will primarily use the agents so we can
    install all of the needed stuff also we need it to come preloaded with
    the stuff an agent will need and depending on the questionaire what tools
    to install for the user ie the stuff in the high quality projects for
    linting typing styling etc".
    - **The base agent toolset is in every node and every OS image,** pinned
      in one manifest (`deploy/toolset/base.json`: each tool's version,
      source and SHA-256).
      - **Tools:** git, gh, the runtime's pinned Node LTS (24), Python 3 (with
        uv), ripgrep, fd, jq, curl, unzip, build-essential and clang, make
        and cmake, and gitleaks.
      - **Our bundled skills:** the vendored high-quality-projects package
        (`project_setup`, `quality_retrofit`, `feature_delivery`, with its
        scripts and templates, M89/D68) and the first-party skills. They are
        on the Model API backend's `bundled` source, and installed for Muse
        Code by the same logic as `bundledSkillsInstall.ts`, moved to a
        portable module the runtime can call.
      - **The `/help` reference.**
      - **Chrome for Testing for agents** comes through M81's verified store,
        fetched at first boot under the same consent as M81's download, since
        Google's terms govern its binaries (decision 26). It is pinned per
        release, not baked into an image.
      - **Where it lives.** On a home node the toolset is in the container,
        run as the tools' user (decision 23). From M110b it is the default
        sandbox image. On Muse Node OS it is the sandbox image too, never the
        read-only host (decision 24).
      - **Size.** It adds an estimated 500–700 MB compressed to the node's
        200 MB runtime base. Lane B0 measures both and records them as
        separate budgets.
    - **A first-run questionnaire** in the first-boot setup (the web UI, the
      TUI, and M111's desktop onboarding with its owner), and again from
      **Settings › Set up for my work**.
      - **How the user will mostly use the agents** (several may be chosen):
        web and TypeScript; Python and data; Rust; C and C++; C# and .NET;
        Go; Java and Kotlin; mobile; makers and embedded (M103); DevOps and
        containers; docs and writing; game development.
      - **Experience level** (new to this, comfortable, expert). It sets how
        much the agents explain, and whether a new project starts in Plan
        mode. It never changes approvals, paid consent, sandboxing or any
        safety rule.
      - **How strict the quality defaults are.**
        - **Strict:** the skill's full gate set, recommended.
        - **Standard:** format, lint, types, tests and secrets; dead code and
          duplication offered later.
        - **Light:** format, secrets and tests.

        This is a default the `project_setup` flow proposes for the user's
        projects. It never loosens a project that already has gates.

      - **The answers** are kept in `profile.json` beside `node.json`: not
        secret, shown in Settings, changeable at any time. They pre-fill
        `project_setup`'s interview as the user's stated defaults, and the
        skill still asks its own questions.
      - **Then a list, never a silent install.** The answers map to packs
        (below). The setup shows each pack with its tools, versions, licences,
        download and disk size, and where it downloads from. The user ticks
        what to install; nothing installs until **Install**.
    - **Toolchain packs, from the skill's stack table**
      (`vendor/high-quality-projects-skill/skills/project_setup/SKILL.md`,
      Phase 2, and its cross-cutting tools):

      | Pack                      | Runtime and SDK                                            | Gate tools                                                                                                                                                                                   | Chosen by                     |
      | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
      | TypeScript and JavaScript | Node 24 and 22, npm, pnpm through Corepack                 | prettier, eslint with typescript-eslint `strictTypeChecked`, tsc strict, knip (plain `knip`, `knip.jsonc`), dpdm (not madge), npm audit, semgrep, vitest; stylelint and htmlhint for the web | web and TypeScript, mobile    |
      | Python                    | CPython through uv                                         | ruff (format, `ALL`), mypy strict, vulture, deptry, bandit, pip-audit, pytest                                                                                                                | Python and data               |
      | Rust                      | rustup with a pinned toolchain, and nightly for sanitizers | rustfmt, clippy pedantic, cargo-machete, cargo-audit, cargo-deny                                                                                                                             | Rust                          |
      | C and C++                 | clang and gcc, CMake, Ninja                                | clang-format, clang-tidy, cppcheck, ASan and UBSan builds, valgrind, ctest                                                                                                                   | C and C++, game development   |
      | C# and .NET               | the .NET SDK (LTS)                                         | dotnet format, analyzers at `latest-all`, NuGetAudit, dotnet test                                                                                                                            | C# and .NET, game development |
      | Go                        | the Go toolchain                                           | gofmt, go vet, Staticcheck, govulncheck, go test                                                                                                                                             | Go, DevOps                    |
      | Java and Kotlin           | a Temurin JDK (LTS), Gradle, Maven                         | ktlint, detekt, Checkstyle, SpotBugs, JUnit (M104's gate set; the skill's table has no JVM row)                                                                                              | Java and Kotlin, mobile       |
      | Shell and PowerShell      | bash, PowerShell 7                                         | shfmt, shellcheck, bats; PSScriptAnalyzer, Pester                                                                                                                                            | DevOps, every stack           |
      | DevOps and containers     | Podman, Helm, kubectl, OpenTofu                            | actionlint, zizmor, hadolint, a Helm schema check                                                                                                                                            | DevOps and containers         |
      | Docs and writing          | —                                                          | prettier, markdownlint-cli2, Vale, a link checker                                                                                                                                            | docs and writing              |
      | Mobile                    | the Android SDK command-line tools                         | the TypeScript or JVM pack's gates; Android lint                                                                                                                                             | mobile                        |
      | Makers                    | Python                                                     | PlatformIO, esptool, arduino-cli, picotool, mpremote; optional emulators (QEMU, Renode; Wokwi's CLI needs the user's own token, D83.14)                                                      | makers and embedded           |
      | Game development          | Godot (headless)                                           | the C# or C++ pack's gates; Godot's own checks                                                                                                                                               | game development              |
      | Cross-cutting (always)    | —                                                          | gitleaks, semgrep, jscpd, OSV-Scanner                                                                                                                                                        | every answer                  |
      - **What cannot be equal is said.** iOS development needs macOS and
        Xcode, so a Linux node offers the cross-platform parts and says so.
        Unity's editor has its own licence and is not a pack.

    - **How packs install.**
      - **Pinned, and checked for compatibility first.** The pack index pins
        every tool's exact version and digest. Before installing, the
        installer checks each pack's declared constraints against the others
        and against the project's own lockfile. This is the skill's "verify
        compatibility" rule, made a check:
        - The TypeScript pack pins TypeScript 6.0.x, because typescript-eslint
          8's peer range (`>=4.8.4 <6.1.0` when the skill checked it) would
          otherwise silently disable every type-aware rule. The same reason
          is why this repository pins 6.0.x (AGENTS.md).
        - The TypeScript pack has dpdm, not madge, whose peer range rejects
          TypeScript 6.
        - A conflict refuses the install and names both sides; nothing passes
          `--legacy-peer-deps` or its like.
      - **Layers that come off cleanly.** Each pack is an OCI layer composing
        the sandbox image, on every node form; content-addressed, so two
        workspaces share it. On Muse Node OS the same layers serve Podman's
        sandboxes. System extensions stay for host add-ons only (decision 24).
        **Remove** drops the layer and leaves nothing behind.
      - **A signed pack index,** like the OS's update channel. It is
        cosign-signed by the release workflow, refuses a lower version or
        stale metadata, and every artifact is pinned by digest. Pack layers
        are built in CI from upstream sources by their own pins: npm and uv
        lockfiles with hashes, `cargo install --locked`, and release binaries
        with SHA-256. Each layer carries an SBOM and passes the vulnerability
        scan (M110's gates).
      - **Click-through licences stay the user's.** The Android SDK asks for
        its licence on the device, by the user's click, as Chrome does.
      - **Sizes before install, and an offline cache.** The download and disk
        size are shown before **Install**. Installed layers stay in a cache on
        the state volume under its quota (decision 19), so a re-install or a
        new workspace works offline.
      - **Bounded and visible.** An install is governed background work, kind
        `packInstall` (D87.2): it waits at throttle and pause, and shows
        "waiting: machine busy". It is never silent. Every install, update and
        removal is a user action, logged in the audit.
        - Updates are offered when the signed index changes.
        - A pack's security update can apply by itself only if the user turned
          that on, and then it stages and applies when idle, like the OS.
      - **Agents may ask, never install.** An agent that needs a missing tool
        asks for its pack with a card naming the pack, its size and its
        licence. Only the user's click installs it.
    - **Agents know what is installed.**
      - **A capability file** in every sandbox (`/etc/muse/toolchains.json`,
        zod-validated) lists each installed pack, its tools and versions, and
        each stack's gate commands. The commands come from the skill's table
        and its "flags that make a linter a gate", for example `eslint
--max-warnings=0`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` and `semgrep scan
--error`.
      - **Agents read it through a read-only `toolchains` tool,** and Muse
        Code through the runtime's MCP server, as with D83.16's maker tools.
        One stable line in the system context names it. It changes only when
        packs change, so the prompt cache stays warm (the SoL-Pi invariants),
        and a node with no packs sends byte-identical requests.
      - **Checks stay approved commands.** M68's verify loop proposes the gate
        commands for the project's stack from the file. The user approves
        them as checks, and a peer still cannot send a command string (D80.4).
      - **"Set up this project" uses the skill as written.** `project_setup`
        and `quality_retrofit` find the package's `templates/` and
        `detect-stack` scripts at the vendored package root (D68's
        `SKILL_ROOT` line). They copy the pre-tuned configs, and run the
        gates with tools the capability file says are present. A missing
        tool becomes a pack request, never a guessed install.
    - **The same questionnaire for the user's own machine** (lane TV,
      optional). In VS Code and every other editor, through the panel and the
      companion page (D84), the same questions can produce a guided install
      list for the user's own computer. It shows the commands for that OS
      (winget, Homebrew, apt), with the same pinned versions and the same
      compatibility check. Each command runs only when the user clicks it, in
      a terminal they see, followed by a version check. The extension
      installs nothing by itself.
    - **Amended 2026-10-05: personas get an experience, not only a pack.**
      The owner: "if in the questionnaire the user is for like coding devices
      ie esp and raspberry pi i would like a way to simulate what they would
      need … sort of the same way i want for the web dev mode to be
      comfortable for a web dev i want that user to be accommodated by
      experience and software as well and the same goes for others you can
      think of that will be using this os", and "any of this should be easy to
      also setup later as well if they want".
      - **The questionnaire's first question becomes ten personas** (several
        may be chosen): makers and embedded; web; data and ML; mobile;
        backend and DevOps; game and graphics; systems (C, C++, Rust);
        security and CTF; docs and writing; learning and students. The
        languages become the second question (TypeScript, Python, Rust, C and
        C++, C# and .NET, Go, Java and Kotlin), pre-ticked from the personas.
        Both map to the packs above.
      - **Each persona installs its packs and turns on an experience:** a
        workbench layout, sidebar sections, preview and view modes,
        simulators, a sample project, and an agent role (M96's charters) and
        skills tuned for that work. Web development (D91.23, M111w) is the
        model; every persona gets the same depth. D91's amendment lists each
        persona's experience; M111x builds them.
      - **An experience is a declarative manifest** (packs, layout,
        simulators, role, skills, checks, its sample and what its TUI view
        offers), signed in the pack index, so a new persona is data, not
        code. Several combine; where two set the same layout slot, the
        first chosen wins and the setup says so.
      - **Set up later, any time, without reinstalling.** The questionnaire
        re-runs from **Settings › Experiences**, the launcher's **Add
        experience…**, the TUI's menu and `muse-experience add <name>` (with
        `remove` and `list`). A later setup uses the installer's themed,
        guided flow: progress, the tips gallery, resumable downloads, and
        rollback on failure.
      - **Removing an experience removes only what it alone added.** Packs and
        simulators are reference-counted across experiences; a pack another
        experience or the user installed stays.
      - **The agent may propose one, never install one.** On a matching
        project (an `sdkconfig` or `platformio.ini`, an `AndroidManifest.xml`,
        a `project.godot`…) it asks once, as an M112 question: "This looks like
        an ESP32 project. Set up the Makers experience?", with **Set up**
        (which opens the guided flow, where nothing installs before
        **Install**), **Not now**, and a remembered choice for such projects:
        Ask (the default), Always open the setup, or Never suggest.
      - **The same everywhere:** accessibility, the 14 languages, the theme,
        and GUI and TUI parity where it makes sense (D91's amendment says
        where it does not).
      - **Tested** per persona in the image CI (M110os and M111os): the
        sample project builds and runs in its simulator on first boot; add,
        then remove, then add again leaves the same state.
    - **Amended 2026-10-06: the local judge, offered at install.** The owner:
      "during the os install there should be a scan to see if the device can
      accommodate the local model judge and if yes ask the user if they would
      like to install during installation and this should also download the
      proper model install it and configure it in our interface to work
      properly on nodes and on hosts".
      - **Exactly M98's local judge, nothing new.** D77's separate local
        judge is a decision model on Ollama's `/v1/systemone` loopback route:
        `tev1:4b` is the recommended model on CPU and GPU, `tev1:0.8b` the
        smaller one, and general models of at least 3B judge through logprobs
        (D77, "Two sources" and its probe table; research in
        `docs/certification/m98-research.md`: Ollama 0.35.1 on
        `127.0.0.1:11434`, `tev1:4b` Q8_0 4.5 GB, `tev1:0.8b` Q8_0 811 MB).
        Phase 2j builds it after its design spike, from D77's carried design:
        the pinned `node:net` transport, the per-connection provenance
        checks (the peer process is Ollama's own binary at its install path;
        the served model's weights are on this disk and match the digest),
        consented pulls, and `museSpark.judge.engine`'s `auto` resolving to
        `both` once a verified separate judge is installed. The install step
        builds on that runtime and that model family, and is shown only once
        2j's verdict is outcome (a), verified local inference, and 2j has
        merged.
      - **One scan, before the questionnaire's downloads,** in every install
        path: M111i's graphical installer, Muse Node OS's first-boot setup
        and the headless installer ISO's pages (OS3), and `node init` for a
        container or native install (the TUI and the CLI). It reads:
        - RAM, and free RAM;
        - the GPU's vendor and VRAM, and the backend the pinned Ollama can use
          on it: CUDA (with OS5's NVIDIA add-on), ROCm, Metal on Apple silicon
          (the native macOS node, M110g), Vulkan where the pin supports it,
          or none; inside a container only what CDI passes in (M110g);
        - CPU features: AVX2 or AVX-512 on x86-64, NEON on ARM64;
        - free disk on the target.
        - **A micro-benchmark,** optional and skippable: 10 to 20 seconds
          (`JUDGE_BENCH_BUDGET_MS`, 20,000) of prompt processing and one warm
          judgment with the smallest candidate (`tev1:0.8b`), in the live
          session or after the base system is installed. It needs that model's
          download, so it is offered with its size; declined or offline, the
          recommendation rests on the hardware alone and says "speed not
          measured". A model the benchmark fetched is kept only if it is the
          one chosen.
      - **The recommendation** comes from a committed table
        (`src/shared/judgeModels.json`, zod-checked): each row is a model and
        quantization from the Ollama library's published tags, with its
        download and resident size, RAM or VRAM need, backends, the warm
        latency per state measured on the rigs (the Kubuntu CPU and the GTX
        1080 Ti, as in D77), and a judge-quality note from D77's table
        (`tev1:4b`: 0.975 on the 40-item set; `tev1:0.8b`: 0.750, ten misses,
        offered only where `tev1:4b` cannot run, and labelled lower quality).
        Each row names its source and check date. A device is recommended
        when the model fits with `JUDGE_MEMORY_HEADROOM_GIB` (1.5) to spare and
        without crossing M107's free-memory floor, and its expected warm
        latency is within `JUDGE_STATE_LATENCY_MAX_MS` (5,000); otherwise the
        scan says "not recommended on this device" with the reason in plain
        words ("needs 6 GB of free memory; this device has 4 GB").
      - **One choice** on the questionnaire page, shown only when the scan
        recommends: "Install the local judge (about {size} to download, runs
        on your {GPU/CPU}, about {minutes} to set up)". On by default when
        recommended (the enhancements-on ruling); nothing downloads before
        **Install**, which is the consent D77's consented pulls ask for.
        **Advanced:** another size from the table, CPU only, or skip. The
        model's licence (read from its official card by lane TJ and
        recorded) is shown, with an accept step if its terms require one: the
        user clicks it, never us.
      - **Download and install.** The pinned Ollama release comes from its
        GitHub release with its SHA-256 (rule 9), as an add-on layer per
        architecture and backend (OS5's system-extension mechanism on Muse
        Node OS; M110g's loopback sidecar recipe in a container). The model's
        manifest and blobs come from the Ollama registry by digest, resumable
        by range and verified by SHA-256, through the installer's download
        manager (M111i's ID; TP2's on a node), with the gallery while it
        waits, written into the runtime's model store on the target. The
        runtime runs as an unprivileged `muse-judge` service user, in a
        sandboxed unit, on loopback only, with all other network denied (it
        never needs one: we fetch, it serves), so the judge never phones home
        and has no telemetry.
      - **Configure.** On the host (Muse Desktop) and on every node, the judge
        is registered as the local separate judge: the endpoint, the model id
        and its digest, the runtime's path for 2j's provenance check, and the
        limits (the loaded context window, one request at a time, the
        timeout). A **health check** then sends one judgment of a fixture with
        a known answer and shows the result and its latency. If anything
        fails, the install carries on without the judge and Settings › Judge
        offers **Set up later**, the same flow (decision 27's later-setup
        rule).
      - **A node's judge for its orchestrator.** Once M100 has merged, a node
        can serve its judge to its orchestrator over the paired channel,
        admitted by the node's M107 governor (a `judge` governed kind, with
        M107's owner), and labelled "on {node}". As D77 keeps confidential
        workspaces local-only, a paired node's judge is never used in one.
      - **After install,** Settings › Judge (the node's web UI and TUI, Muse
        Desktop's settings app, and, through the same module, M98's own
        setup in every editor) shows the model, its size, the hardware and
        backend, **Update**, **Remove** (the runtime layer and the blobs it
        alone added), **Re-scan**, and the last health check.

**Suggested additions** (not in the owner's words; each with its reason):

- **The local gateway** (decision 12): the remote web UI on the user's own
  loopback. _Reason:_ no public web port, no domain, no certificate, and the
  browser never talks to a third party.
- **A node can be its owner's blind relay** (decision 8). _Reason:_ two NATs
  need a meeting point, and the user's own rented server is one that sees
  only ciphertext, with no service of ours.
- **Model requests relayed through the orchestrator** (decision 7). _Reason:_
  API keys never reach a rented server, and D89.13's "values never travel"
  still holds.
- **Approval forwarding with per-action binding** (decision 10). _Reason:_
  D80.8 deferred it, and a node with nobody at it cannot work without it.
- **A commitment-based SAS, not a bare short code** (decision 9). _Reason:_
  without a commitment, a man in the middle can try keys until two short
  strings match.
- **Revocation and stop from any device, subtract-only** (decisions 9 and
  15). _Reason:_ a lost laptop has to be cut off from the phone in your hand;
  subtract-only commands are safe to accept from any pair.
- **Sealed at boot, unsealed from a paired device** (decision 9). _Reason:_
  a provider that snapshots or reboots the server gets nothing usable.
- **The metadata address blocked in every sandbox** (decision 5). _Reason:_
  on most clouds it hands out the instance's credentials to any process.
- **Per-workspace egress allowlists and DNS logs** (decision 5). _Reason:_
  the cheapest limit on what a prompt injection can send out.
- **Crypto-erase on wipe** (decision 19). _Reason:_ a provider's disk cannot
  be trusted to erase; destroying the keys first can be.
- **Clock checks** (decision 19). _Reason:_ certificates, TOTP and journal
  ordering all fail quietly with a wrong clock.
- **Caps and retention on everything** (decision 19). _Reason:_ the GitHub
  Actions storage incident; a node that fills its disk stops working.
- **A native node on macOS** (decision 4). _Reason:_ Apple's GPU cannot reach
  a Linux container.
- **Remote actuation only from a surface within sight** (decision 14).
  _Reason:_ a person approving motion from another city cannot see who is
  standing next to the machine.
- **Pi realism: 64-bit OS, 8 GB, an SSD** (decision 4). _Reason:_ SD cards
  wear out under journals and builds, and 32-bit images cannot run the CLIs.
- **Team mode as its own phase** (decision 16). _Reason:_ vendors' terms bind
  subscriptions and keys to one person; sharing a node is a terms question
  before it is a code question.
- **Workers dial out** (decision 8). _Reason:_ the commonest setup (a laptop
  and a rented server) then needs no listener on the laptop and no relay.
- **Signed, reversible upgrades** (decision 15). _Reason:_ a node far away
  that fails an upgrade must come back by itself.
- **An optional code-server pack** (decision 17). _Reason:_ some people want a
  full VS Code in the browser; code-server is MIT and takes our extension from
  Open VSX, where VS Code's own server may not be hosted.
- **Other agents' sign-in tokens never enter the vault** (decision 7).
  _Reason:_ Anthropic, Google and OpenAI each forbid or warn against a third
  party holding them; only API keys are brokered.
- **Outbound connection limits per sandbox** (decision 5). _Reason:_ rented
  servers' providers lock servers that scan other networks.
- **The browser pairing installs the node's own certificate** (decision 23).
  _Reason:_ browsers refuse passkeys behind a clicked-through warning, and a
  self-signed, non-CA certificate can vouch for nothing but the node.
- **Two users in one container for the first phase** (decision 23).
  _Reason:_ it keeps the node's keys and sessions out of the tools' reach on
  Docker Desktop, where nested sandboxes are not available.
- **Chrome for Testing for agents, installed Chrome for people** (decision
  26). _Reason:_ automation needs a pinned, verified build and a throwaway
  profile; the user's Chrome holds their sign-ins and updates itself.
- **A kiosk session on the host's own screen** (decision 26). _Reason:_ it
  gives a machine with a monitor a trusted local browser, which also solves
  browser sign-ins on a node.
- **The skill's compatibility rule as a check before every pack install**
  (decision 27). _Reason:_ the newest TypeScript silently disables
  typescript-eslint's type-aware rules; a check catches it, and a habit does
  not.
- **Packs as shared, content-addressed layers with an offline cache**
  (decision 27). _Reason:_ ten workspaces should not download a toolchain ten
  times, and a re-install should work without a network.
- **Agents ask for a pack; they never install one** (decision 27). _Reason:_
  an install changes the machine and fetches code, which is the user's call.
- **A capability file and a `toolchains` tool** (decision 27). _Reason:_
  agents that guess the gate commands produce decorative gates.
- **Experience level never touches safety** (decision 27). _Reason:_ a
  beginner needs the same approvals and sandbox as an expert, with more
  explanation.
- **Per-pair rotating discovery tokens** (decision 25). _Reason:_
  broadcasting a node's id on the LAN would let anyone there track it.
- **The node dials home on an address change** (decision 25). _Reason:_ the
  side whose address changed knows first; waiting for the other side to
  rediscover it is what cost 25 minutes.
- **Epoch-fenced gates for every effect that leaves a sandbox** (decision
  25). _Reason:_ a lease alone cannot stop a node that comes back late; the
  gates refuse its old epoch, so re-dispatch never runs an effect twice.
- **Turn resilience is harness-wide, not node-only** (decision 25).
  _Reason:_ the turn that failed that night was an ordinary agent's; every
  editor needs the pause-and-resume.
- **Raspberry Pi Imager's cloud-init seed for first-boot Wi-Fi** (decision
  24). _Reason:_ a Wi-Fi-only machine has no network on which to show a setup
  page, and people already know Imager's settings dialog.
- **A setup code on the console, not first-come setup** (decision 24).
  _Reason:_ the appliances we looked at let whoever reaches the page first
  become the owner.
- **An add-on layer of system extensions** (decision 24). _Reason:_ Chrome
  and NVIDIA's driver cannot be in a signed, read-only image, but must still
  update and roll back cleanly.
- **Network-bound disk unlock from the user's own orchestrator** (decision
  24). _Reason:_ a headless machine without a TPM otherwise waits at boot for
  someone to type a passphrase.
- **OS security updates staged at once, applied only when idle** (decision
  24). _Reason:_ unattended updates must never reboot a node in the middle of
  a task.
- **The exact source packages published with each OS image** (decision 24).
  _Reason:_ the images carry GPL software, and distributing binaries carries
  the duty to offer their source.
- **Peek's local part ships before the node** (decision 22). _Reason:_ the
  Agent map and the TUI already run subagents and team workers on one
  machine; nothing in a local peek needs a node.
- **"Values never travel" amended only for "My node" pairs** (decision 10).
  _Reason:_ the owner wants D89's modes over the channel for his own nodes,
  and a pair with another person's device should keep D89.13's stricter
  rule.

### D91 — Muse Desktop: the host edition's own shell (M111, 2026-10-05)
